---
title: "Background: zonotope propagation"
subtitle: "Why boxes lose information when a set is pushed through a step map, what a zonotope is, which operations on it are sound and why, and how each check of a certified funnel becomes a check on a zonotope."
lightbox: true
---

**What this explains.** Every certificate on these pages is a statement
about a *set* of states: a box of poses on which contacts hold the box, a
band of a [certified funnel](funnels.qmd), an entry set, an exit set. Today
the certifier stores all of them as boxes and pushes them through the
dynamics by interval arithmetic. This page shows the two ways that loses
information, introduces the zonotope, proves the handful of operations a
certifier needs, and then maps each condition of our funnels onto those
operations. You need a little linear algebra and the mean value theorem.

**Where this is going.** A zonotope set type is being built into the
certifier's core, and it is the planned replacement for the interval
machinery. Boxes are a special case of zonotopes, so the replacement can
happen one edge at a time. The landing's impact window, where intervals
fail, is its first client. The set representation for mode-branched sets
is the hybrid zonotope of Koeln and colleagues, and that line is being
pursued with them.

## 1. Intervals, and the two ways they lose

An **interval** $[x]=[\underline x,\overline x]$ is a closed bounded set of
reals, and a **box** is a vector of intervals. Interval arithmetic replaces
each operation by the set of its results, rounded outward:
$$
[x]+[y]=[\underline x+\underline y,\ \overline x+\overline y],\qquad
[x]-[y]=[\underline x-\overline y,\ \overline x-\underline y],
$$
and a product takes the least and largest of the four endpoint products.

**Why it is sound.** Evaluate an expression with every operation replaced
by its interval version: the result contains the expression's value at
every point of the box. That is induction over the expression, since each
interval operation contains every result of the operation on its
arguments. This *inclusion property* is the whole basis of every interval
certificate here, however coarse the result is.

**Loss 1: dependency.** Interval arithmetic treats each occurrence of a
variable as a new, independent variable. For $[x]=[0,1]$,
$$
[x]-[x]=[0-1,\ 1-0]=[-1,1],
$$
although $x-x=0$ for every $x$. Inside one formula the mean-value form
(the value at the centre plus an interval gradient times the half-widths)
removes most of this.

**Loss 2: wrapping.** A step of a dynamical system maps a box to a set that
is usually *not* a box. The next step only accepts a box, so the image is
replaced by its **interval hull**, the smallest box around it. The hull
adds corners the true set does not have, and the next step maps those
corners too. The loss compounds over the steps.

::: {.callout-tip title="Worked example: a rotation by 45°"}
Let each step rotate the plane by $45°$ and start from the square
$[-1,1]^2$. The rotated square has its corners on the axes at distance
$\sqrt2$, so its interval hull is $[-\sqrt2,\sqrt2]^2$. Rotating a box of
half-width $h$ and boxing it again gives half-width $\sqrt2\,h$, every
step. After 8 steps, two full turns, the box is $[-16,16]^2$, while the
true set is the original square again. The rotation is an isometry; the
factor 16 in width (256 in area) comes from nothing but the choice to
store boxes.
:::

![Eight rotations by 45° of the square [−1, 1]². (a) Re-boxed sets after k = 1, …, 4 steps (blue) and the zonotope, which is the exact set at every step (orange; filled: k = 0). (b) Half-widths on a log scale: the re-boxed interval grows by √2 per step, to 16 after 8 steps; the zonotope's own interval hull alternates between 1 and √2. Drawn by `reports/technical-report/scripts/ch18_wrapping.py`.](media/bg_zonotope_wrapping.png){.lightbox}

Splitting boxes (bisection) fights wrapping only by brute force. In the
landing's impact window it would need about 10<sup>10</sup> pieces.

## 2. Zonotopes

A **zonotope** has a centre $c\in\R^n$ and a generator matrix
$G=[g_1,\dots,g_m]\in\R^{n\times m}$:
$$
\mathcal Z(c,G)=\{\,c+G\xi:\ \xi\in[-1,1]^m\,\}.
$$
It is a sum of $m$ segments, so it is a centrally symmetric polytope. Three
special cases:

- **A box** is $\mathcal Z(c,\operatorname{diag}(r))$ with half-widths $r$.
  Every interval certificate is already a zonotope certificate with a
  diagonal $G$.
- **A parallelepiped** ($m=n$, $G$ invertible) is the set form of Lohner's
  method for validated ODE solutions, which keeps a rotated coordinate frame
  from step to step.
- **A segment** is a zonotope with one generator.

### Affine maps and sums are exact

$$
A\,\mathcal Z(c,G)+b=\mathcal Z(Ac+b,\ AG),\qquad
\mathcal Z(c_1,G_1)\oplus\mathcal Z(c_2,G_2)=\mathcal Z(c_1+c_2,\ [G_1,G_2]).
$$
*Why:* $A(c+G\xi)+b=(Ac+b)+(AG)\xi$ for every $\xi$, and stacking
$(\xi_1,\xi_2)$ ranges over the bigger cube exactly when each part ranges
over its own. Nothing is lost. A linear step costs one matrix product, and
the rotation example is resolved: $R^8\mathcal Z(0,I)=\mathcal Z(0,R^8)=
\mathcal Z(0,I)$.

### Affine arithmetic is zonotopes, one operation at a time

Affine arithmetic writes each quantity as $\hat x=x_0+\sum_i x_i\epsilon_i$
with **noise symbols** $\epsilon_i\in[-1,1]$ shared by all quantities. A
vector of such forms *is* a zonotope: the $x_0$'s are the centre and the
coefficient columns are the generators. Shared symbols cancel, so
$\hat x-\hat x=0$ exactly: the dependency loss is gone. A nonlinear
operation becomes its best affine approximation plus one *new* noise
symbol that bounds the error. A zonotope step does the same for a whole
step map at once.

### Nonlinear steps: linear part plus a remainder

Let $f$ be the step map and $X=c+[-r,r]$ the zonotope's interval hull, with
$r=|G|\,\mathbf 1$ (row sums of $|G|$). Linearize at the centre and append
the error as new generators.

**Lagrange form.** If $[H_j]$ bounds the Hessian of $f_j$ on $X$, then
$$
f(\mathcal Z(c,G))\subseteq\mathcal Z\big(f(c),\ [\,J_f(c)\,G,\ \operatorname{diag}(e)\,]\big),
\qquad e_j=\tfrac12\, r^\top\big|[H_j]\big|\,r .
$$
*Why:* for $x=c+G\xi$, Taylor's theorem gives
$f_j(x)=f_j(c)+\nabla f_j(c)\cdot G\xi+\tfrac12\,\delta^\top H_j(\zeta)\,\delta$
with $\delta=G\xi$, $|\delta|\le r$ and $\zeta$ on the segment from $c$ to
$x$, inside the convex set $X$. The last term is at most $e_j$.

**Mean-value form.** If $[J]$ bounds the Jacobian on $X$, with midpoint $M$
and radius $\Delta$, then
$f(\mathcal Z)\subseteq\mathcal Z(f(c),\,[MG,\ \operatorname{diag}(\Delta r)])$.

The **Lagrange remainder is quadratic** in the set's size $r$, with the
Hessian bound as its coefficient. The **mean-value remainder is linear** in
$r$, with the Jacobian enclosure's radius $\Delta$ as its coefficient, and
it carries every overestimate of that enclosure; chained over several steps
those overestimates multiply. In both forms the linear part $JG$ keeps
every correlation the set had, which is exactly what re-boxing throws away.
Floating-point rounding is bounded and appended as one more diagonal block.

### Order reduction

Every nonlinear step appends generators, so they have to be capped. Split
$G=[G_1,G_2]$ and replace the second part by its interval hull:
$$
\mathcal Z(c,G)\subseteq\mathcal Z\big(c,\ [\,G_1,\ \operatorname{diag}(|G_2|\,\mathbf 1)\,]\big).
$$
*Why:* $\mathcal Z(c,G)=\mathcal Z(c,G_1)\oplus\mathcal Z(0,G_2)$, and the
second term lies in its interval hull. Girard's rule boxes the generators
that lose least when boxed, so the loss stays small and controlled.

### The closed-form check

$$
\min_{x\in\mathcal Z(c,G)} a\cdot x \;=\; a\cdot c-\big\|G^\top a\big\|_1
\;=\; a\cdot c-\sum_i |a\cdot g_i| .
$$
*Why:* $a\cdot(c+G\xi)=a\cdot c+\sum_i(a\cdot g_i)\,\xi_i$ with independent
$\xi_i\in[-1,1]$, and each term is least at
$\xi_i=-\operatorname{sign}(a\cdot g_i)$. So "is $a\cdot x\ge b$ on the whole
set?" is one line of arithmetic, no linear program. A nonlinear quantity
$q(x)\ge b$ is checked as its linearization plus a remainder:
$q(c)-\|G^\top\nabla q(c)\|_1-e\ge b$.

### Containment

- **In a half-space or a box: exact.** $\mathcal Z(c,G)$ lies in
  $\{a\cdot x\le b\}$ exactly when $a\cdot c+\|G^\top a\|_1\le b$; for a box
  $[l,u]$ that is $c-|G|\mathbf 1\ge l$ and $c+|G|\mathbf 1\le u$.
- **In another zonotope: a sufficient linear test.** If
  $G_1=G_2\Gamma$, $c_1-c_2=G_2\beta$ and every row of $[\Gamma,\beta]$ has
  absolute sum at most 1, then $\mathcal Z(c_1,G_1)\subseteq\mathcal
  Z(c_2,G_2)$, since $c_1+G_1\xi=c_2+G_2(\beta+\Gamma\xi)$ and
  $|\beta+\Gamma\xi|\le 1$ componentwise. It is one linear program; exact
  zonotope containment is hard in general.

### Constrained and hybrid zonotopes

A contact guard is a half-space (a gap $\phi(x)\le 0$), and a zonotope cut
by a half-space is no longer a zonotope. A **constrained zonotope**
$\{c+G\xi:\ \xi\in[-1,1]^m,\ A\xi=b\}$ is closed under such cuts; its checks
become linear programs. At an impact the set splits into branches, one per
contact mode. A **hybrid zonotope** adds binary factors
$\xi^b\in\{-1,1\}^{n_b}$: it is the union of $2^{n_b}$ constrained
zonotopes with shared generators, carried as one set, and its checks are
mixed-integer linear programs, one LP per branch when the branches are few.

## 3. Applied to our certifier

**An edge certificate is set reachability.** An edge of a funnel is the
closed loop
$$
x_{k+1}=f\big(x_k,\ \pi(x_k),\ \theta,\ \sigma_k\big),
$$
with $x$ the state along the edge, $\pi$ the feedback law, $\theta$ the
uncertain parameters and $\sigma_k$ the contact mode. The friction band
$\mu\in[0.3,0.5]$ becomes **one extra generator** (half-length 0.1 about
0.4) on a state that never changes; scene parameters and the measured
disturbances become further generators. The mode is the planned one, and
the certificate proves Coulomb's law selects it: closed contacts stay
closed, open ones stay open, normal forces stay positive, sliding forces
sit on the cone edge opposite the slip.

**Every condition is a closed-form check.**

- the **contact-force floor**: each closed contact's normal force at least
  $N_{\min}$;
- the **friction cones**: $0.3\,\lambda_n\pm\lambda_t>0$ for a sticking disk,
  with $\mu\lambda_n$ for sliding contacts linearized (its bilinear part goes
  into the remainder);
- the **motor box**: four linear checks on the commanded force;
- the **reading condition**: each recognizer clause compares a gap, a
  distance or an angle with its band edge, one scalar check each;
- progress, slip signs and slip bounds, and the mode's equations staying
  nonsingular.

**Junctions are containment checks.** A junction composes when the exit set
*certified* for one edge lies in the entry set *certified* for the next.
Measured entry sets, joint 95/95 regions of the states MJX actually
reaches, are subsets of the executed states and are used only to validate
coverage; composition is established on certified sets. The entry set is a
design choice: take the previous edge's certified exit and re-verify the
next funnel's bands from it, and containment holds by construction.

**Boxes are the diagonal case.** A box exit is a valid zonotope entry as it
stands, and a zonotope exit is checked against a box entry exactly. Interval
certificates and zonotope certificates therefore compose with **no loss at
the hand-off**, and edges can move to zonotopes one at a time.

**The impact window is the first client.** Six entry coordinates, five to
seven steps, an impact with indeterminate impulses and a contact switch:
everything that makes re-boxing fail. The zonotope carries the state through
the steps before the impact, splits at the guard into the impact's branches
(constrained zonotopes, or one hybrid zonotope over all of them), and
follows each branch to rest.

**Learned proposals, checked exactly.** A certificate's free choices (the
entry set's generators, which generators order reduction keeps, how the
guard is split) can come from anywhere, including the graph network that is
planned to propose certificates per edge. The verifier checks each proposal
with the lemmas above. A bad proposal can make a certificate fail; it can
never make a false one pass.

## 4. What the records show so far

One experiment: one impact branch, one $0.02\times0.02$ mm entry sub-box,
and a first-order form (a chain-rule product of interval Jacobians)
intersected at every step with the re-boxed set. It is the mean-value form
above, not yet generator matrices or the Lagrange form.

- **The make step** encloses the reached set 2<sup>8.8</sup>–2<sup>12.6</sup>
  times tighter in volume than re-boxing.
- **The steps before the impact** gain little.
- **The tail step**, alone, is 2<sup>8.7</sup>–2<sup>12.7</sup> times
  looser: the product of interval Jacobians overestimates the tail's stiff
  rows. The intersection with the re-boxed set carries it.
- **The decision number, 2<sup>12</sup>,** is *not* a shrinkage of the
  reached set. It is the growth, in volume, of the entry boxes on which every
  rocking class after the impact is excluded: from 2<sup>−4</sup> to
  2<sup>−2</sup> of the entry box per coordinate, over six coordinates,
  against a bar of 2<sup>10</sup> set beforehand.

::: {.callout-warning title="Day-1 results: to be added"}
The first results of the zonotope set type itself (generator matrices, the
Lagrange remainder, order reduction, guard splitting) on the impact window
will be added here when they land.
:::

## 5. Related work

**The foundation.** Hybrid zonotopes
([Bird, Pangborn, Jain and Koeln, *Automatica* 2023](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.automatica.2023.111107)),
their nonlinear successor sets
([Siefert et al., ACC 2023](https://doi.org/10.23919/ACC55779.2023.10156300)),
functional decomposition
([Siefert et al., arXiv 2304.06827](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.06827)) and
the zonoLAB toolbox
([Koeln et al., arXiv 2310.15426](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.15426)) are
what this route builds on for mode-branched sets; constrained zonotopes
([Scott et al., *Automatica* 2016](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.automatica.2016.02.036))
are their continuous part.

**Methods, not the problem.** Zonotopes against the wrapping effect go back
to [Kühn (*Computing*, 1998)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02684450);
Lohner's method is surveyed by
[Nedialkov, Jackson and Corliss (1999)](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0096-3003(98)10083-8);
[Girard (HSCC 2005)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-31954-2_19) made
zonotopes the reachability set for uncertain linear systems and gave the
order reduction used here; affine arithmetic is
[de Figueiredo and Stolfi (2004)](https://doi.org/10.1023/B:NUMA.0000049462.70970.b6).

**How this differs from other reachability and funnel work.**
[CORA](https://doi.org/10.29007/zbkv) and
[polynomial zonotopes](https://doi.org/10.1145/2461328.2461358),
[Flow*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-39799-8_18) and
[Taylor models](https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1024467732637), and
[mixed-monotone](https://doi.org/10.1145/2728606.2728607) and
[immrax](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ifacol.2024.07.428) interval embeddings
compute reachable sets of *given* dynamics and guards.
[Polytopic trees](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICRA.2019.8793634) with
[linear containment encodings](https://doi.org/10.1109/CDC40024.2019.9029363),
[mixed-integer planning through contact](https://doi.org/10.1109/HUMANOIDS.2017.8239534),
[LQR-trees](https://doi.org/10.1177/0278364910369189) and
[funnel libraries](https://doi.org/10.1177/0278364917712421) plan with
funnels or with modes fixed in the model. Here the contact modes are
decided by Coulomb friction over an uncertain friction band and certified
along with the funnel; the modes change the object's contacts with its
environment; the funnels are chained on a contact-formation graph and
checked against MJX; and learned proposals are verified exactly.
